1.explanation:
• audits/byte-efficiency/unused-css-rules-test.js: Contains tests for measuring unused CSS, directly related to the “Defer unused CSS” audit that is mis-reporting sizes.
• audits/byte-efficiency/uses-text-compression-test.js: Tests around gzip compression checks; relevant because the bug is that gzip compression is not being taken into account for injected CSS.
• audits/byte-efficiency/total-byte-weight-test.js: Tests for byte-weight calculations on resources—helps understand how raw sizes vs. compressed sizes are computed.
• gather/dobetterweb/response-compression-test.js: Verifies logic for detecting and measuring compressed responses; relevant to how Lighthouse infers gzip savings.
• computed/network-analysis-test.js: Provides coverage for network analysis utilities that translate network requests into size estimates; shows how Lighthouse reads networkRecord metadata and compression ratios.
• network-records-to-devtools-log.js: Utility for transforming network records into DevTools log format in tests; useful for reproducing and mocking gzipped network responses in unit tests.
1.bug_scenario: When running Lighthouse (via Google PageSpeed Insights) on a page that loads CSS via a third-party JavaScript tool—fetching styles as gzipped JSON (~20 KB) and then injecting them into a <style> tag—Lighthouse’s “Defer unused CSS” audit reports the inline CSS size as ~80 KB (and 70 KB savings), because it measures the raw uncompressed CSS in the DOM rather than the actual gzipped resource size. The screenshot highlights an entry for “body.mopinion-modal-active { overflow: hidden !important } …” showing 80 KB size and 70 KB potential savings, which overestimates the real network cost.
